status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly stated the manuscript 'made an important and interesting contribution meriting publication' and did not challenge the core findings about opposite effects of distance-dependent versus uniform contrast reduction on speed perception. The main experimental results showing speed overestimation in fog and underestimation with uniform contrast reduction were accepted, with revisions requested only for methodological clarifications and discussion of limitations.

Reviewers raised significant concerns about ecological validity, noting the scenes 'had impoverished detail compared to real life driving' with few landmarks, traffic signs, or obstacles. They requested discussion of 'the extent to which the driver's ability to estimate self-motion speed could be affected by the choice of stimuli compared to a real driving scenario.' This indicates uncertainty about whether the findings generalize beyond the simplified experimental conditions, though the design choice itself was understood as intentional to isolate perceptual effects.

Reviewers expressed concern that 'the presentation of the statistics should make it clearer how the data were analyzed and which differences were significant.' They noted that 'error bars are presented but are unspecified' and 'the specifics of the ANOVAs are missing (factorial or not; outcome of main effects and interactions).' This indicates the statistical evidence was present but insufficiently transparent for full evaluation, requiring clarification rather than additional data.

Reviewers questioned whether haptic feedback was truly eliminated, asking 'the revised manuscript should describe the extent to which the haptic feedback from the steering wheel gave the driver information about vehicle speed' and noting 'a slight rotation of the steering wheel at 20 km/h will have a different effect on the simulated car position in the scene than the same rotation at 120 km/h.' They asked 'could the drivers be using this information to help formulate their speed judgements?' This raises uncertainty about whether a potential confound was adequately controlled.

The anti-fog manipulation and its opposite effects compared to normal fog were not specifically challenged by reviewers. These findings were part of the 'important and interesting contribution' that reviewers accepted for publication. No concerns were raised about the validity of the anti-fog results themselves, only about general methodological transparency and ecological validity that applied to all experiments.

The relationship between perceived speed and driving behavior was not questioned by reviewers. The consistent pattern across perception and production experiments was implicitly accepted as part of the manuscript's 'important and interesting contribution.' Reviewers focused on methodological details rather than challenging the perception-behavior link demonstrated across experiments.

Reviewers raised concerns about prolonged experimental sessions, asking 'the revised manuscript should discuss the extent to which contrast adaptation could affect performance over the trials' and whether there was 'evidence for sequence effects over trials (e.g. from the beginning to the end of a session) that could be related to prolonged exposure to different contrast levels.' They specifically questioned why 'trials in Exp. 4 last so long (3 x 5 trials over 1.5 hrs).' This indicates uncertainty about potential confounds from adaptation effects that may not have been adequately addressed.
